title: Repeated MFA prompts — question explanation
learningObjective: Recognize repeated push prompts as possible account compromise and deny/report them
format: 16:9 educational motion-graphics video; narration; separate captions; no autoplay with sound
visualStyle: Deep navy and charcoal; restrained cyan/electric-blue highlights; limited purple accents; clean typography; purposeful, low-motion transitions; accessible contrast.

scenes.name: Scenario setup
scenes.visual: Over ten minutes, your authenticator sends repeated sign-in approval prompts. You are not attempting to sign in, and a coworker says to approve one to stop them.
scenes.direction: Show a fictional simulated setting. Use generic UI and no actual organization, brand, user identity, credential, real URL or live account.

scenes.name: Learning objective and risk cue
scenes.visual: Recognize repeated push prompts as possible account compromise and deny/report them
scenes.direction: Highlight only observable cues and explain the decision context without implying certainty beyond the scenario.

scenes.name: Recommended response
scenes.visual: Option D: Deny the prompts, stop interacting with them and contact the security team immediately. Repeated uninitiated prompts can be authentication fatigue and may indicate a password is already known to an attacker.
scenes.direction: Animate the recommended defensive choice as a clear decision path. Display the action verb and trusted channel/control.

scenes.name: Why the other options fail
scenes.visual: Option A: Disabling MFA removes a protection and does not address the attempted sign-in. Option B: Public disclosure may reveal account details and will not trigger formal incident response. Option C: Approving may complete an attacker’s login; later action may be too late.
scenes.direction: Show each unsafe alternative separately with a complete, concise reason. Do not depict operational exploitation, malicious code or credential capture.

scenes.name: Defensive takeaway
scenes.visual: Deny every uninitiated prompt and report immediately. Follow the identity team’s instructions for password reset, session revocation and authenticator review. Repeated uninitiated prompts are a possible compromise signal, not a harmless notification problem.
scenes.direction: Close with one readable takeaway and the next safe action. Keep the final frame long enough for comprehension.

narration: Scenario: Over ten minutes, your authenticator sends repeated sign-in approval prompts. You are not attempting to sign in, and a coworker says to approve one to stop them. Safest response: Option D: Deny the prompts, stop interacting with them and contact the security team immediately. Repeated uninitiated prompts can be authentication fatigue and may indicate a password is already known to an attacker. Option A is unsafe because Disabling MFA removes a protection and does not address the attempted sign-in. Option B is unsafe because Public disclosure may reveal account details and will not trigger formal incident response. Option C is unsafe because Approving may complete an attacker’s login; later action may be too late. In practice: Deny every uninitiated prompt and report immediately. Follow the identity team’s instructions for password reset, session revocation and authenticator review. Key takeaway: Repeated uninitiated prompts are a possible compromise signal, not a harmless notification problem.
